Next steps for pilot expansion and on-prem sizing
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-05-14
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Atlas CTO), Diego Marquez (Atlas ML Eng), Priya Singh (Atlas Infra)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh quick check-in, we have about 45 minutes, agenda is benchmark review versus your baseline provider, go over tuning notes and action items
[00:18] Sara Patel: hi thanks Maya, yep excited to see the numbers, Diego sent over the baseline earlier
[00:25] Liam O'Connor: morning all, I'll start with a quick recap of test setup, we ran 3 load profiles — steady, bursty 10x, and tail spike; models used were rdx-7b-quant for Redwood and baseline was using vendor-A's 7B variant, config notes in the spreadsheet link we sent
[00:48] Diego Marquez: small note, baseline included a custom prompt cache on their side, so keep that in mind
[00:55] Liam O'Connor: yeah good call, we attempted to mirror that with our KV cache but there may be slight differences
[01:10] Maya Chen: ok Liam, can you walk p50/p95 numbers first
[01:15] Liam O'Connor: sure, p50 for steady state — Redwood: 85ms, baseline: 120ms; p95 Redwood: 420ms, baseline: 400ms; p99 Redwood: 980ms, baseline: 920ms — so we beat p50, matched p95-ish but we're slightly higher on p99 during artificial tail blasts
[01:42] Priya Singh: is the p99 difference consistent or only on synthetic spikes?
[01:46] Liam O'Connor: mostly on synthetic tail spikes where KV cache invalidations and cold KV miss amplified latency; normal production-like traffic we saw p99 around 850-900ms
[02:00] Diego Marquez: what was token length distribution? could that explain tail behavior
[02:07] Liam O'Connor: yes we used the sample prompts Diego provided — average token output ~ 60 tokens, 95th ~240 tokens; longer sequences amplify kernel selection overhead which affects tail
[02:25] Sara Patel: cost numbers — how do we look on per-token cost compared to baseline?
[02:30] Maya Chen: we projected two scenarios — hosted pay-as-you-go and reserved. For your bursty usage, with intelligent batching and prefix cache we estimate 30-40% lower unit cost versus baseline for identical throughput; reserved capacity pushes that to ~50% in your steady case
[02:52] Diego Marquez: is that including egress and network costs for private deployment?
[02:58] Maya Chen: good question, those top-line numbers are inference compute + model serving overhead; we added a separate line for expected egress and top-of-stack networking which is small relative to compute but will vary by region — we'll put full line items in the spreadsheet
[03:18] Priya Singh: Security — can you confirm KMS integration and audit logs for Private? Our compliance team needs HSM-backed key support
[03:25] Liam O'Connor: we support customer-managed keys via major KMS providers; HSM integrations are available for Private deployments and we can supply audit log schema, retention and sampling for SOC2 purposes
[03:38] Sara Patel: are there any known gaps in RBAC or SSO we should expect?
[03:43] Maya Chen: SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported; RBAC is role-based with audit trails — we'll share the security pack after the call
[03:50] Diego Marquez: back to latency — what tuning knobs did you try to reduce p99?
[03:54] Liam O'Connor: three main levers: (1) aggressive KV prefetching for common prefixes, (2) adaptive batching with a short latency budget for p99-sensitive routes, (3) model quantization tradeoffs — we ran q4 followed by mixed int8 runs. Prefetching reduced p99 on steady traffic by ~12% in our runs
[04:18] Sara Patel: any accuracy differences with quantization? We care about hallucination rates a bit for clinical text
[04:24] Liam O'Connor: negligible for most of your eval prompts at q4; we did a small eval sweep on your 200 prompt set — rouge/emd delta <1.5% — full eval results in the spreadsheet
[04:39] Diego Marquez: can you remind us about fallback policies if a dedicated node is down or saturated
[04:45] Maya Chen: smart routing: requests are routed by policy to dedicated, hosted or cheaper variants; automatic fallback to compatible model variants and region-level failover; SLA response is backed in Dedicated contracts
[04:58] Priya Singh: for on-prem we'll need a sizing doc — how many GPUs for our 1k qps burst profile?
[05:04] Liam O'Connor: rough ballpark from today: for 1k qps with avg tokens 60, and our batching settings you'll need ~8 A100-equivalent GPUs for steady plus 4 more for 10x burst headroom; we'll produce formal on-prem sizing after we ingest your 24h traffic
[05:22] Diego Marquez: the baseline provider claims they get better tail by using micro-sharding, did you try that approach
[05:27] Liam O'Connor: not exactly micro-sharding, but we did kernel-level parallelism and async kv loads; micro-shard helps but increases inter-GPU comms and cost — tradeoff worth exploring for p99-sensitive endpoints
[05:44] Sara Patel: let's talk about SLA — what uptime/latency guarantees can we expect on Dedicated vs Hosted during pilot
[05:51] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and target latency windows; hosted API has best-effort SLOs but we offer prioritized capacity for pilots and a burst pool; we'd need to commit if you want hard SLAs
[06:06] Priya Singh: if we go private, how long to provision a VPC/on-prem package? We have a compliance cutover in Q3
[06:12] Liam O'Connor: VPC private deployment typically 6-8 weeks from kick-off for standard topologies; on-prem will depend on hardware procurement but we can parallelize the sizing work now
[06:25] Maya Chen: taking us back to the numbers — Diego any concerns with the sheets so far?
[06:29] Diego Marquez: looks good but p99 needs more repeatability; can you re-run runs with a cold start schedule and longer warmup so we can see steadier tails
[06:40] Liam O'Connor: absolutely, planning 3 more runs — cold-start, warm-start, and a mixed-hour trace matching your traffic spikes; will report back by Monday
[06:51] Sara Patel: ok sounds good, also we'd like cost ramp projections for reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go across 3, 6, 12 months
[06:59] Maya Chen: we'll include that; rough numbers today looked favorable but we'll formalize
[07:06] Priya Singh: one more question on observability: what traces/metrics do you provide out of the box for token-level billing and latency per-route
[07:12] Liam O'Connor: console exposes token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, KV hit/miss rates, and trace IDs — you can export to your telemetry stack; we'll share sample dashboards
[07:27] Diego Marquez: can you add a column in the spreadsheet for KV hit rate per run? that would help diagnose p99
[07:34] Liam O'Connor: yes will add KV hit/miss, batch size distributions, and region used per run
[07:42] Maya Chen: quick recap and next steps: Redwood to send updated spreadsheet, cost calc, and security pack; SE to run additional tail experiments; Atlas to send 24h traffic and confirm the on-prem kickoff window; schedule infra call for week of 5/19
[07:58] Sara Patel: agreed. thank you
[08:02] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up, bye

Notes: transcript contains minor transcription artifacts, names sometimes appear with small typos. Shared artifacts: benchmark_spreadsheet.xlsx (link in CRM), security_pack.pdf (link), pilot_sow_draft.pdf (link).
questions: How does Redwood's p99 compare on realistic cold-start traffic?
What are the cost tradeoffs of reserved capacity vs pay-as-you-go for bursty workloads?
Does Redwood support HSM-backed KMS for Private deployments?
